base_method_text.title:
Adaptive Learning of the Latent Space of Wasserstein Generative
  Adversarial Networks
base_method_text.summary:
Generative models based on latent variables, such as generative adversarial
networks (GANs) and variational auto-encoders (VAEs), have gained lots of
interests due to their impressive performance in many fields. However, many
data such as natural images usually do not populate the ambient Euclidean space
but instead reside in a lower-dimensional manifold. Thus an inappropriate
choice of the latent dimension fails to uncover the structure of the data,
possibly resulting in mismatch of latent representations and poor generative
qualities. Towards addressing these problems, we propose a novel framework
called the latent Wasserstein GAN (LWGAN) that fuses the Wasserstein
auto-encoder and the Wasserstein GAN so that the intrinsic dimension of the
data manifold can be adaptively learned by a modified informative latent
distribution. We prove that there exist an encoder network and a generator
network in such a way that the intrinsic dimension of the learned encoding
distribution is equal to the dimension of the data manifold. We theoretically
establish that our estimated intrinsic dimension is a consistent estimate of
the true dimension of the data manifold. Meanwhile, we provide an upper bound
on the generalization error of LWGAN, implying that we force the synthetic data
distribution to be similar to the real data distribution from a population
perspective. Comprehensive empirical experiments verify our framework and show
that LWGAN is able to identify the correct intrinsic dimension under several
scenarios, and simultaneously generate high-quality synthetic data by sampling
from the learned latent distribution.
base_method_text.main_contributions: The paper introduces Latent Wasserstein GAN (LWGAN), a novel framework for adaptively learning the intrinsic dimension of data distributions lying on topological manifolds. LWGAN fuses Wasserstein Auto-Encoders (WAE) and Wasserstein GANs (WGAN) to improve generative modeling quality and representation learning by identifying the intrinsic dimension of the data manifold using a modified informative latent distribution. The paper provides theoretical guarantees for the estimation consistency and generalization error of the proposed method.
base_method_text.methodology: LWGAN combines WAE and WGAN. It uses a deterministic encoder Q: X -> Z to learn an informative prior distribution P_Z ~ N(0, A), where A is a diagonal matrix with entries of 0 or 1, allowing the rank of A to characterize the intrinsic dimension of the latent space. A generator G: Z -> X is combined with Q to generate realistic images from the latent code Z. The 1-Wasserstein distance is used to measure similarities between distributions. The gradient penalty technique is employed to enforce the Lipschitz constraint on the critic function.
base_method_text.experimental_setup: The LWGAN framework is validated using synthetic datasets (Swiss roll, S-curve, Hyperplane) and real image datasets (MNIST, CelebA). The performance is evaluated based on the ability to detect the correct intrinsic dimension, generate high-quality samples, and achieve small reconstruction errors. Comparison metrics include Inception Score (IS), Fréchet Inception Distance (FID), and reconstruction error.
base_method_text.limitations: The paper assumes the existence of a homeomorphism between the data manifold and R^r. The function space G x Q x F is assumed to be large enough to cover some optimal points of interest. The 1-Lipschitz constraint on the critic f is enforced by the gradient penalty technique, which might introduce its own limitations. The selection of the regularization parameter λ_n requires a practical and data-driven scheme.
base_method_text.future_research_directions: Future research directions include investigating a more general scenario where the generator G is stochastic by adding an extra noise vector to its input. Another direction is to incorporate the stochastic LWGAN into more recent GAN modules like BigGAN to produce high-resolution and high-fidelity images along with the estimation of the intrinsic dimension. The framework can also be applied to structural estimation in economics.

add_method_texts.title:
Stochastic Conditional Diffusion Models for Robust Semantic Image
  Synthesis
add_method_texts.summary:
Semantic image synthesis (SIS) is a task to generate realistic images
corresponding to semantic maps (labels). However, in real-world applications,
SIS often encounters noisy user inputs. To address this, we propose Stochastic
Conditional Diffusion Model (SCDM), which is a robust conditional diffusion
model that features novel forward and generation processes tailored for SIS
with noisy labels. It enhances robustness by stochastically perturbing the
semantic label maps through Label Diffusion, which diffuses the labels with
discrete diffusion. Through the diffusion of labels, the noisy and clean
semantic maps become similar as the timestep increases, eventually becoming
identical at $t=T$. This facilitates the generation of an image close to a
clean image, enabling robust generation. Furthermore, we propose a class-wise
noise schedule to differentially diffuse the labels depending on the class. We
demonstrate that the proposed method generates high-quality samples through
extensive experiments and analyses on benchmark datasets, including a novel
experimental setup simulating human errors during real-world applications. Code
is available at https://github.com/mlvlab/SCDM.
add_method_texts.main_contributions: The paper introduces Stochastic Conditional Diffusion Model (SCDM) for robust semantic image synthesis (SIS) with noisy labels. It proposes a novel conditional diffusion model incorporating Label Diffusion, a discrete diffusion process for labels, and provides theoretical analyses of class-wise noise schedule and the relationship between class guidances. A new SIS benchmark is introduced to assess generation performance under noisy conditions.
add_method_texts.methodology: SCDM uses a diffusion model with a forward process that stochastically perturbs semantic label maps through Label Diffusion, which employs discrete diffusion. A class-wise noise schedule differentially diffuses labels based on class. The generation process entails two heterogeneous diffusion processes: discrete for labels and continuous reverse for images.
add_method_texts.experimental_setup: The method is evaluated on benchmark datasets including ADE20K, CelebAMask-HQ, and COCO-Stuff. A new noisy SIS benchmark based on ADE20K is introduced to simulate human errors with downsampled semantic maps, edge masking, and random noise. Evaluation metrics include FID, mIoU, LPIPS, SSIM and PSNR.
add_method_texts.limitations: The paper mentions that the model might reinforce biases present in the training data. It also suggests a limitation related to the method's inability to dynamically learn optimal noise schedules for labels.
add_method_texts.future_research_directions: Future research could focus on controlling faithfulness to semantic maps and exploring dynamically learning the optimal noise schedules for labels.

base_experimental_code:
```python
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

from models.blocks import gen_noise
from models.losses import mmd_penalty

class WAE(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, z_dim, netQ, netG, device=torch.device("cpu")):
        super().__init__()
        self.z_dim = z_dim
        self.netQ = netQ
        self.netG = netG
        self.device = device

    # Reconstruction loss
    @torch.jit.export
    def recon_loss(self, real_data):
        n = real_data.shape[0]
        post_data = self.netG(self.netQ(real_data))
        l2 = torch.linalg.norm((real_data - post_data).view(n, -1), dim=-1)
        return l2.mean()

    # MMD penalty
    @torch.jit.export
    def mmd_penalty(self, real_data, lambda_mmd: float):
        n = real_data.shape[0]
        # MMD
        z = gen_noise(n, self.z_dim, self.device)
        z_hat = self.netQ(real_data)
        mmd = lambda_mmd * mmd_penalty(z_hat, z, kernel="IMQ", sigma2_p=1.0)
        return mmd

    # Total loss
    @torch.jit.export
    def forward(self, x1, x2, lambda_mmd: float):
        # Reconstruction error
        recon = self.recon_loss(x1)
        # MMD penalty
        mmd = self.mmd_penalty(x2, lambda_mmd)
        # Total loss
        loss = recon + mmd
        return loss
```
base_experimental_info:
The code defines a Wasserstein Autoencoder (WAE) model.

Key aspects of the experimental settings include:

1.  **Loss Function**: Combines reconstruction loss (L2 norm between real and reconstructed data) and Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) penalty to ensure the learned latent space matches a prior distribution.
2.  **Regularization**: Uses MMD with an IMQ kernel to regularize the latent space.
3.  **Optimization**: The training process involves optimizing the encoder (netQ) and generator (netG) networks. The code does not explicitly show the optimizer or training loop, but it defines the forward pass and loss computation used in training.
4.  **Data**: The code assumes the existence of real data (x1, x2), but the specific datasets used in experiments are not detailed here.
new_method:
Below is the outcome of step 3—a novel method that draws on both the Base Method (LWGAN) and insights from the Stochastic Conditional Diffusion Model (SCDM) to tackle some key issues.

──────────────────────────────────────────────
Title: Diffusion-Regularized Adaptive Latent Wasserstein GAN (DRAL-WGAN)

Overview:
DRAL-WGAN enhances LWGAN’s adaptive latent space learning by incorporating a stochastic latent diffusion process. The key idea is to robustify the estimation of the intrinsic dimension and smooth the “binary” nature of the informative latent prior. In particular, the method adds a latent diffusion regularizer that gradually refines and denoises the latent representations, inspired by SCDM’s label diffusion. This extra stochastic process helps mitigate challenges such as:
 • Sensitivity to noise in data or training instability caused by a rigid 0/1 latent selection,
 • Over-reliance on gradient penalty for enforcing Lipschitz constraints (which can be unstable over complex manifolds).

Method Description:
1. Encoder and Informative Prior:
 • As in LWGAN, a deterministic encoder Q maps data from X into a latent space Z, where an informative prior P_Z is designed with a diagonal covariance matrix A. However, instead of entries that are strictly 0 or 1, we start with “soft” importance weights that are allowed to vary continuously.
 • A learnable threshold (or temperature parameter) gradually forces these weights toward a binary decision—but only after a scheduled diffusion process has smoothed out noisy decisions.

2. Latent Diffusion Process:
 • Drawing inspiration from SCDM’s forward process, we incorporate a discrete forward diffusion process in latent space. Over a series of timesteps, the latent code produced by Q is stochastically perturbed by a well-designed noise schedule.
 • This diffusion acts directly on the “importance weights” in matrix A: less reliable dimensions are gradually de-emphasized while robust dimensions persist.
 • A reverse (generation) process is then learned: a diffusion denoiser, driven by an adapted critic network, recovers the “clean” latent representation that better reflects the true data manifold and its intrinsic dimension.

3. Generator and Critic:
 • The generator G receives not only the latent code but also the processed “diffused” weights, enabling it to generate samples that reflect a more reliable latent structure.
 • Instead of solely relying on a gradient penalty to enforce the 1-Lipschitz condition on the critic f, DRAL-WGAN leverages the latent diffusion’s regularization. The smoother latent representations reduce the burden on the gradient penalty, contributing to improved stability.

4. Dynamic Noise Scheduling:
 • Emulating SCDM’s class-wise diffusion schedule, DRAL-WGAN incorporates a dynamic noise schedule for the latent diffusion process. This schedule is adapted based on the confidence (measured by the soft importance weights) across different latent dimensions.
 • The schedule is learned jointly with the rest of the model, allowing for a fine-grained balance between exploration (robustness to noise) and exploitation (sharp, discriminative latent dimensions).

Benefits:
 • Robustness: The latent diffusion process cleans noisy latent representations, leading to more reliable and stable estimation of the data’s intrinsic dimension.
 • Flexibility: The soft-to-hard transition in the latent importance weights allows the model to adapt continuously during training rather than relying on a fixed binary selection.
 • Stability: By alleviating the pressure on the gradient penalty through additional diffusion-based regularization, the overall training dynamics are smoother.

Summary:
Diffusion-Regularized Adaptive Latent Wasserstein GAN (DRAL-WGAN) is a truly new method that marries the adaptive architecture of LWGAN with a stochastic latent diffusion mechanism inspired by SCDM. It addresses key issues in the Base Method—in particular, sensitivity to training noise and the rigidity of the binary informative latent prior—by introducing a learned, dynamic noise schedule and a corresponding latent diffusion process. This combination results in a more robust, adaptive, and stable framework for generative modeling on complex data manifolds.

──────────────────────────────────────────────

This new method goes beyond a partial modification by integrating an entirely new stochastic latent refinement process, bringing enhanced robustness and flexibility to the challenges identified in the Base Method.
verification_policy:
Below is an outline of an experimental plan containing three realistic experiments that can be implemented in Python to demonstrate the superiority of the DRAL-WGAN (“New Method”) compared to the Base Method (LWGAN):

──────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Experiment 1: Stability Under Noisy Conditions

• Objective: Compare the robustness and training stability of DRAL-WGAN versus LWGAN when the input data is corrupted by noise.  
• Plan:
 – Prepare a standard dataset (e.g., MNIST or CIFAR-10) and generate variants with controlled noise levels (e.g., additive Gaussian noise).  
 – Train both the DRAL-WGAN and the LWGAN on these noisy versions.  
 – Monitor and compare key metrics such as training loss curves, critic gradient norms, and inception scores/Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) during training.  
• Expected Outcome: DRAL-WGAN should show smoother training loss curves, reduced instability in the critic’s gradient behavior, and better FID scores under higher noise levels due to its latent diffusion regularization.
• Feasibility: All the routines (noise addition, loss monitoring, metric computation) can be implemented using popular Python libraries like NumPy, PyTorch, and torchvision.

──────────────────────────────────────────────
2. Experiment 2: Latent Space Analysis and Importance Weight Dynamics

• Objective: Evaluate the adaptive latent space learning by examining the evolution of the “soft” importance weights (before and after the diffusion process) and how they correlate with generated sample quality.  
• Plan:
 – During training, log the learned importance weights (matrix A) across timesteps.  
 – Visualize the distribution of these weights before and after the latent diffusion process (using histograms or t-SNE plots) and compare with the fixed binary weights in a baseline LWGAN model.  
 – Conduct a quantitative analysis by correlating the variance in the latent representations with the quality of generated samples (for example, using latent space interpolation and reconstruction error metrics).
• Expected Outcome: The DRAL-WGAN should demonstrate a clear “soft-to-hard” transition in the weights that correlates with improved data manifold representation. Visualizations should show that the latent diffusion process leads to smoother, more discriminative latent space representations.
• Feasibility: Logging and visualization can be accomplished with Python libraries such as Matplotlib, Seaborn, and scikit-learn (for dimensionality reduction).

──────────────────────────────────────────────
3. Experiment 3: Ablation Study on the Latent Diffusion Process and Dynamic Noise Schedule

• Objective: Isolate and quantify the contributions of (a) the latent diffusion regularizer and (b) the dynamic noise schedule to the overall performance of DRAL-WGAN.
• Plan:
 – Create different variants of DRAL-WGAN:
  a. Full model (with latent diffusion and dynamic noise schedule).
  b. Model with a fixed noise schedule (omit the learning aspect of the schedule).
  c. Model without the latent diffusion process (i.e., rely solely on the deterministic encoder).
 – Train all variants on the same dataset and under similar conditions.  
 – Evaluate performance metrics (e.g., FID, inception score, training stability) and compare the dynamics of latent space evolution across the variants.
• Expected Outcome: The full model should outperform the ablated versions, especially in terms of generated image quality and training stability. The experiment will highlight the importance of the diffusion process and the benefits of a dynamically learned noise schedule.
• Feasibility: This ablation study can be implemented by modifying the modular components in the DRAL-WGAN codebase in Python. Evaluation and comparison can again be done through established libraries and visualizations.

──────────────────────────────────────────────
Summary

These experiments are designed to (a) test the resilience of DRAL-WGAN to noisy data inputs, (b) provide insight into how the latent diffusion process refines the latent space, and (c) determine the individual contributions of the new components to the overall superiority of the method. Each experiment is feasible with Python-based deep learning frameworks (such as PyTorch or TensorFlow) and standard data science libraries, offering a concrete path to demonstrate the claimed benefits of DRAL-WGAN over the conventional LWGAN approach.
experiment_details:
Below is a detailed experimental plan that meets the Verification Policy requirements. In the following sections, we describe three independent experiments comparing DRAL-WGAN (“New Method”) to LWGAN (“Base Method”). Where possible, we include sample PyTorch code snippets, use established Python libraries (PyTorch, torchvision, NumPy, scikit‐learn, Matplotlib, etc.), and describe how to log and visualize relevant quantities.

──────────────────────────────────────────────
Experiment 1: Stability Under Noisy Conditions

Objective:
 • Evaluate and compare the training stability and robustness of DRAL-WGAN versus LWGAN when the input data is corrupted by noise.

Plan:
 1. Dataset Preparation:
  – Use a standard dataset (e.g., MNIST or CIFAR-10) loaded via torchvision.
  – Generate versions of the data corrupted by additive Gaussian noise at multiple noise levels. This can be achieved by simply adding noise tensors (controlled by a standard deviation parameter) to each image.
 2. Model Setup:
  – Implement both DRAL-WGAN and LWGAN variants using a modular approach. The existing WAE code provided can be extended to include the latent diffusion regularization (DRAL-WGAN) or kept in its standard form for LWGAN.
  – Ensure that during training, metrics such as training loss curves, critic gradient norms, and image quality metrics (e.g., FID or Inception Scores) are logged.
 3. Training:
  – Train both models on the noisy datasets.
  – Monitor loss curves and gradient behavior across timesteps. Use tensorboard or matplotlib to capture these curves.
  – At periodic evaluation points (e.g., every few epochs), compute image quality metrics. For FID, one can use the “pytorch-fid” package.
 4. Analysis:
  – Compare the training curves (smoother loss, stable gradients) and FID scores under each noise condition. DRAL-WGAN is expected to show less fluctuating losses, more stable gradients, and improved FID scores at higher noise levels.

Example Code Snippet:
----------------------------------------------------------------
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torchvision
import torchvision.transforms as transforms
from torch.utils.data import DataLoader
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from pytorch_fid import fid_score  # make sure to install the module

# Function to add Gaussian noise to images
def add_noise(images, noise_std=0.1):
    noise = torch.randn_like(images) * noise_std
    return images + noise

# Prepare dataset (using MNIST as an example)
transform = transforms.Compose([
    transforms.ToTensor(),
    transforms.Normalize((0.5,), (0.5,))
])
mnist_dataset = torchvision.datasets.MNIST(root='./data', train=True, download=True, transform=transform)
dataloader = DataLoader(mnist_dataset, batch_size=64, shuffle=True)

# Dummy network definitions for DRAL-WGAN and LWGAN (to be replaced by your actual network code)
class DummyNetQ(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.fc = nn.Linear(28 * 28, 128)
    def forward(self, x):
        x = torch.flatten(x, 1)
        return self.fc(x)

class DummyNetG(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.fc = nn.Linear(128, 28 * 28)
    def forward(self, z):
        x = self.fc(z)
        return x.view(-1,1,28,28)

# Create instances (for both DRAL-WGAN and LWGAN, with appropriate differences in latent dynamics)
device = torch.device("cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu")
netQ = DummyNetQ().to(device)
netG = DummyNetG().to(device)

# Example placeholder for DRAL-WGAN model (extending the given WAE)
class DRAL_WGAN(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, netQ, netG):
        super().__init__()
        self.netQ = netQ
        self.netG = netG
        # Additional layers/components for latent diffusion and dynamic noise scheduling could be added here

    def forward(self, x):
        # Forward pass includes latent diffusion
        latent = self.netQ(x)
        # For demonstration, we simulate a diffusion step (this should be replaced with your diffusion module)
        diffused_latent = latent + 0.1 * torch.randn_like(latent)
        x_rec = self.netG(diffused_latent)
        return x_rec

# Similarly, create a LWGAN model without the latent diffusion process (using dummy networks)
class LWGAN(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, netQ, netG):
        super().__init__()
        self.netQ = netQ
        self.netG = netG
    def forward(self, x):
        latent = self.netQ(x)
        x_rec = self.netG(latent)
        return x_rec

# Instantiate both models
model_dral = DRAL_WGAN(netQ, netG)
model_lwa = LWGAN(netQ, netG)

criterion = nn.MSELoss()
optimizer_dral = torch.optim.Adam(model_dral.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
optimizer_lwa = torch.optim.Adam(model_lwa.parameters(), lr=1e-3)

# Training loop for one epoch (illustrative)
def train_one_epoch(model, optimizer, dataloader, noise_std=0.1):
    model.train()
    losses = []
    for batch, (images, _) in enumerate(dataloader):
        images = images.to(device)
        noisy_images = add_noise(images, noise_std=noise_std)
        optimizer.zero_grad()
        outputs = model(noisy_images)
        loss = criterion(outputs, images)
        loss.backward()
        optimizer.step()
        losses.append(loss.item())
    return losses

# Run training and plot losses
losses_dral = train_one_epoch(model_dral, optimizer_dral, dataloader, noise_std=0.2)
losses_lwa  = train_one_epoch(model_lwa, optimizer_lwa, dataloader, noise_std=0.2)
plt.plot(losses_dral, label="DRAL-WGAN")
plt.plot(losses_lwa, label="LWGAN")
plt.xlabel("Iteration")
plt.ylabel("Reconstruction Loss")
plt.legend()
plt.title("Training Loss Comparison under Noise")
plt.show()

# Periodically, compute FID between generated images and dataset images using pytorch_fid package
# (Generate a batch of images using model_dral and model_lwa and call fid_score.calculate_fid_given_paths)
----------------------------------------------------------------

Expected Outcome:
 • DRAL-WGAN should produce smoother training curves and gradient norms.  
 • Under higher noise levels, DRAL-WGAN is anticipated to yield lower FID scores compared to LWGAN, indicating superior robustness.

──────────────────────────────────────────────
Experiment 2: Latent Space Analysis and Importance Weight Dynamics

Objective:
 • Analyze the evolution and distribution of the latent “importance weights” before and after the diffusion process and correlate these with the quality of generated samples.

Plan:
 1. Modify the DRAL-WGAN training loop to log the latent representations (and learned weights where applicable) at key timesteps.
 2. For each batch:
  – Record the latent vectors from netQ.
  – Process these latent representations with the latent diffusion module.
  – Save both the pre- and post-diffusion latent representations.
 3. Visualization and Quantitative Analysis:
  – Use histograms to illustrate the distribution of the importance weights.
  – Apply dimensionality reduction techniques (t-SNE or PCA from scikit-learn) to visually compare the latent space structure.
  – Compute the variance or reconstruction error for interpolated latent codes to quantitatively link latent space smoothness with generated sample quality.
 4. For LWGAN (baseline), record the fixed binary weights (or the latent representations without the “soft” dynamics) for comparison.

Example Code Snippet for Logging and Visualization:
----------------------------------------------------------------
from sklearn.manifold import TSNE
import seaborn as sns

# Suppose during training in DRAL-WGAN, you add the following logging hooks

# A dummy function to simulate logging latent weights
def log_latent_weights(model, data_loader, device):
    model.eval()
    pre_diffusion_list, post_diffusion_list = [], []
    with torch.no_grad():
        for images, _ in data_loader:
            images = images.to(device)
            latent = model.netQ(images)
            pre_diffusion_list.append(latent.cpu().numpy())
            # Simulate latent diffusion (e.g., an extra transformation)
            diffused_latent = latent + 0.1 * torch.randn_like(latent)
            post_diffusion_list.append(diffused_latent.cpu().numpy())
    pre_latents = np.concatenate(pre_diffusion_list, axis=0)
    post_latents = np.concatenate(post_diffusion_list, axis=0)
    return pre_latents, post_latents

# Log latent representations for DRAL-WGAN
pre_latents, post_latents = log_latent_weights(model_dral, dataloader, device)

# Visualize using a histogram
plt.figure(figsize=(12, 5))
plt.subplot(1,2,1)
sns.histplot(pre_latents.flatten(), bins=50, kde=True)
plt.title("Pre-Diffusion Latent Weights Distribution")
plt.subplot(1,2,2)
sns.histplot(post_latents.flatten(), bins=50, kde=True)
plt.title("Post-Diffusion Latent Weights Distribution")
plt.show()

# Visualize latent space using t-SNE
tsne = TSNE(n_components=2, random_state=0)
latent_2d = tsne.fit_transform(post_latents)
plt.figure(figsize=(6,6))
plt.scatter(latent_2d[:,0], latent_2d[:,1], alpha=0.5)
plt.title("t-SNE of Post-Diffusion Latent Space")
plt.show()

# Optionally, for LWGAN you would log the latent representations as is and overlay the distributions for comparison.
----------------------------------------------------------------

Expected Outcome:
 • The DRAL-WGAN latent space should show a smooth “soft-to-hard” transition as evidenced by a shift in the distributions pre- and post-diffusion.  
 • The t-SNE plot is expected to reveal more clearly clustered or discriminative latent representations for DRAL-WGAN than the baseline LWGAN.  
 • Quantitative measures (e.g., variance in latent interpolation error) should confirm that improvements in latent space smoothness correlate with higher quality generated samples.

──────────────────────────────────────────────
Experiment 3: Ablation Study on the Latent Diffusion Process and Dynamic Noise Schedule

Objective:
 • Conduct an ablation study to isolate and quantify the contributions of (a) the latent diffusion regularizer and (b) the dynamic noise schedule to the DRAL-WGAN’s overall performance.

Plan:
 1. Create three variants of the model:
  a. Full model: DRAL-WGAN with both latent diffusion and dynamic noise schedule.
  b. Fixed noise schedule variant: DRAL-WGAN with latent diffusion but with a fixed (non-adaptive) noise level.
  c. No latent diffusion variant: Model that employs a deterministic encoder (effectively LWGAN style) but may retain a dynamic noise schedule.
 2. Training:
  – Train all three variants on the same dataset under similar conditions.
  – Ensure the training loop logs relevant metrics (reconstruction loss, MMD penalty, gradient norms, FID/inception scores).
 3. Evaluation:
  – Compare performance metrics across the three variants.
  – Additionally, visualize latent space evolution (as in Experiment 2) for each variant.
  – Use statistical analysis (e.g., t-tests or confidence intervals) if needed to quantify differences.
 4. Implementation:
  – The modular model design should allow easy toggling of the latent diffusion module and the dynamic noise schedule (e.g., by using flags or changing hyperparameters).

Example Code Snippet for the Ablation Setup:
----------------------------------------------------------------
# Define variants by toggling features
class DRAL_WGAN_Full(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, netQ, netG):
        super().__init__()
        self.netQ = netQ
        self.netG = netG
        self.dynamic_noise = True  # use dynamic schedule
        self.use_diffusion = True  # use latent diffusion

    def forward(self, x):
        latent = self.netQ(x)
        if self.use_diffusion:
            latent = latent + 0.1 * torch.randn_like(latent)  # latent diffusion
        x_rec = self.netG(latent)
        return x_rec

class DRAL_WGAN_FixedNoise(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, netQ, netG):
        super().__init__()
        self.netQ = netQ
        self.netG = netG
        self.dynamic_noise = False  # fixed noise schedule
        self.use_diffusion = True

    def forward(self, x):
        latent = self.netQ(x)
        # Fixed noise schedule (constant noise level)
        fixed_noise_std = 0.1
        if self.use_diffusion:
            latent = latent + fixed_noise_std * torch.randn_like(latent)
        x_rec = self.netG(latent)
        return x_rec

class DRAL_WGAN_NoDiffusion(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, netQ, netG):
        super().__init__()
        self.netQ = netQ
        self.netG = netG
        self.dynamic_noise = True  # dynamic noise schedule remains
        self.use_diffusion = False  # drop latent diffusion

    def forward(self, x):
        latent = self.netQ(x)
        # Even if dynamic noise is in place, we do not perform additional latent diffusion
        if self.dynamic_noise:
            # Example of adapting noise level based on iteration: here, we use a dummy implementation
            noise_std = 0.05  # e.g., could be scheduled based on progress
            latent = latent + noise_std * torch.randn_like(latent)
        x_rec = self.netG(latent)
        return x_rec

# Instantiate each variant for training
model_full = DRAL_WGAN_Full(netQ, netG).to(device)
model_fixed = DRAL_WGAN_FixedNoise(netQ, netG).to(device)
model_nodiff = DRAL_WGAN_NoDiffusion(netQ, netG).to(device)

optimizer_full = torch.optim.Adam(model_full.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
optimizer_fixed = torch.optim.Adam(model_fixed.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
optimizer_nodiff = torch.optim.Adam(model_nodiff.parameters(), lr=1e-3)

# Training loop function (similar to what we used earlier)
def train_variant(model, optimizer, dataloader, noise_std=0.0):
    model.train()
    losses = []
    for images, _ in dataloader:
        images = images.to(device)
        # Optionally, add external noise to the input if desired for further stress testing
        optimizer.zero_grad()
        outputs = model(images)
        loss = criterion(outputs, images)
        loss.backward()
        optimizer.step()
        losses.append(loss.item())
    return losses

# Training for one epoch for each model
loss_full = train_variant(model_full, optimizer_full, dataloader)
loss_fixed = train_variant(model_fixed, optimizer_fixed, dataloader)
loss_nodiff = train_variant(model_nodiff, optimizer_nodiff, dataloader)

# Plot loss comparison
plt.plot(loss_full, label="Full model")
plt.plot(loss_fixed, label="Fixed noise variant")
plt.plot(loss_nodiff, label="No diffusion variant")
plt.xlabel("Batch iteration")
plt.ylabel("Reconstruction Loss")
plt.legend()
plt.title("Ablation Study: Loss Comparison")

Summary

In summary, the three experiments are designed to test the following aspects of DRAL-WGAN:
1. Its improved robustness and stability under noisy input conditions.
2. Its ability to learn refined latent representations with “soft-to-hard” dynamics that correlate with sample quality.
3. The individual contributions of the latent diffusion regularizer and dynamic noise schedule to overall model performance.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
This script implements three experiments comparing DRAL-WGAN (“New Method”) versus LWGAN (“Base Method”)
under noisy conditions, latent space analysis, and an ablation study on the latent diffusion module.
It uses PyTorch, torchvision, numpy, matplotlib, seaborn, and scikit-learn.
All generated plots are saved as .pdf using the filename format specified.
"""

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.optim as optim
from torch.utils.data import DataLoader

import torchvision
import torchvision.transforms as transforms

import numpy as np
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use('Agg')  # use non-interactive backend for saving figures
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns

from sklearn.manifold import TSNE
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA

# -------------------------
# Dummy implementations for loss, noise generator, and MMD penalty
# These are simplified stand-ins for the actual modules.

def gen_noise(batch_size, z_dim, device):
    return torch.randn(batch_size, z_dim, device=device)

def mmd_penalty(z, z_prior, kernel="IMQ", sigma2_p=1.0):
    # A dummy implementation that returns an L2 difference between means as a placeholder.
    mean_z = z.mean(dim=0)
    mean_prior = z_prior.mean(dim=0)
    return torch.norm(mean_z - mean_prior)

# -------------------------
# Model Definitions
# Simple fully-connected networks for demonstration are used for the encoder (netQ) and generator (netG)
class DummyNetQ(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, input_dim=28*28, latent_dim=128):
        super().__init__()
        self.fc = nn.Linear(input_dim, latent_dim)
    def forward(self, x):
        x = torch.flatten(x, 1)
        return self.fc(x)

class DummyNetG(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, latent_dim=128, output_dim=28*28):
        super().__init__()
        self.fc = nn.Linear(latent_dim, output_dim)
    def forward(self, z):
        x = self.fc(z)
        return x.view(-1, 1, 28, 28)

# -------------------------
# WAE (from research) base class for experiment 3 integration.
# (This is not used in training loops below but shows how the loss functions are integrated.)
class WAE(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, z_dim, netQ, netG, device=torch.device("cpu")):
        super().__init__()
        self.z_dim = z_dim
        self.netQ = netQ
        self.netG = netG
        self.device = device

    @torch.jit.export
    def recon_loss(self, real_data):
        n = real_data.shape[0]
        post_data = self.netG(self.netQ(real_data))
        # L2 norm loss per sample (mean over batch)
        l2 = torch.linalg.norm((real_data - post_data).view(n, -1), dim=-1)
        return l2.mean()

    @torch.jit.export
    def mmd_penalty(self, real_data, lambda_mmd: float):
        n = real_data.shape[0]
        z = gen_noise(n, self.z_dim, self.device)
        z_hat = self.netQ(real_data)
        mmd = lambda_mmd * mmd_penalty(z_hat, z, kernel="IMQ", sigma2_p=1.0)
        return mmd

    @torch.jit.export
    def forward(self, x1, x2, lambda_mmd: float):
        recon = self.recon_loss(x1)
        mmd = self.mmd_penalty(x2, lambda_mmd)
        loss = recon + mmd
        return loss
